title: How to Make a Game on iPad for Free

body_markdown:
You can make a real game on an iPad, for free, without writing code. You do not need a Mac, Xcode, or a Unity license.


This guide walks through the whole thing: what you need, how long it takes, and a first game you can finish in an afternoon.


## What You Need to Make Games on iPad


- **An iPad.** Any recent one works. A larger screen helps when you are wiring up logic, but it is not required.
- **hyperPad Starter.** Free, one project, all the building tools.[Download hyperPad Starter.](https://apps.apple.com/app/apple-store/id6737631128?pt=467885&ct=blog&mt=8)
- **About two hours.** That is enough for a playable first game.


A stylus and a keyboard are nice. Neither is necessary.


## How Game Development on iPad Works


In hyperPad you build games out of three things:


- **Scenes.** A screen in your game. A menu is a Scene. A level is a Scene.
- **Objects.** Anything in a Scene. Your player, a platform, a button, a score label.
- **Behaviors.** The logic. You connect actions and events into a flowchart that says what happens when.


That last one replaces code. Instead of writing` if (collision) { score += 1 }` , you drag a collision event, connect it to a Change Attribute action, and set the Attribute to score plus one. Same result, visible on screen.


A few more examples of how Behaviors read:


- When the player taps, jump.
- When the player hits a spike, lose health.
- When a timer ends, spawn an enemy.


## Plan Your Game Before You Build


Five minutes of planning saves an hour of rework.


1. **Think about games you like.** What exactly do you enjoy about them?
2. **Pick a simple concept.** Classic arcade games like "Pong" or "Flappy Bird" are good models for a first project.
3. **Sketch it on paper.** Draw the main character, the obstacles and the goal.


Then answer three questions:


- **Objective:** What is the player trying to do? Reach the end of a level, collect every item, or survive for a set time.
- **Controls:** How does the player play? Tap, swipe or tilt.
- **Levels:** Is it one endless screen, or separate levels?


Every game needs a simple loop: the player moves, avoids or interacts with something, and then wins or loses. Get that loop working before anything else.


## Make Your First Game on iPad, Step by Step


This builds a simple tapper. It is small enough to finish and complete enough to feel like a game.


Prefer to watch first? This video walks through building a game in hyperPad.


https://www.youtube.com/embed/ae6hmCb8SQQ?si=E7_aSZMsPy8CUJvS


### 1. Start a new project


Open hyperPad and create a new project. Pick a blank Scene. You now have an empty game.


Want a head start instead? Choose a template. Templates come with movement, a camera setup and basic UI already built, and a simple platformer template is a quick way to learn how the pieces fit.


### 2. Add your player Object


Open the Asset Dock and drag in a Graphic. The built-in library has characters, platforms, and UI pieces, so you do not need to make art first. Drop one into the Scene and it becomes an Object.


### 3. Make it respond to a tap


Select the Object and open the Behavior Editor.


- Add a **Touch** event.
- Connect it to a **Move** action.
- Set the movement to a short upward hop.


Hit play. Tap the screen. Your Object moves. That is your first working Behavior, and you did not type anything.


### 4. Add gravity


Turn on physics for the Object and give it gravity. Now the hop falls back down on its own. Adjust the hop strength until it feels right. This is the part that takes the longest, and it is the part that decides whether the game feels good.


### 5. Add something to avoid


Drag in a second Object as an obstacle. Give it a **Move** Behavior so it scrolls from right to left, and a **Spawn** Behavior so a new one appears every couple of seconds.


### 6. Handle the collision


On your player, add a **Collided** event that checks for the obstacle. Connect it to an action that ends the game, or restarts the Scene.


### 7. Add a score


Add a Label Object. Create an Attribute called score. Every time an obstacle passes the left edge, add one to score and update the Label.


### 8. Test on the device you built it on


Press play and actually play it. This is the part iPad development gets right. There is no build step and no simulator, so the loop between changing something and feeling the change is a few seconds.


Each time you play, look for three things:


- **Bugs:** anything that doesn't work the way you expected.
- **Difficulty:** too easy, too hard, or about right?
- **Clarity:** is it obvious what the player should do?


Most of a game's quality comes from this loop of small tweaks.


### 9. Polish


Add a sound on the tap, a different sound on the collision, and a title screen as a second Scene. Small touches, large difference.


### 10. Share it


When it plays well, publish it to the Hub and send it to a few friends. Real players notice things you didn't, and their feedback shapes your next version.


**Ready to build this one?**[Download hyperPad Starter](https://apps.apple.com/app/apple-store/id6737631128?pt=467885&ct=blog&mt=8) and follow along. It is free and it covers a full project.


## Free Art, Sound, and Tools


You can import your own graphics, sounds, music and fonts into hyperPad, including drawings you make in Procreate. If you'd rather not make everything yourself, these free resources help:


- **Graphics and sprites:**[OpenGameArt.org](https://opengameart.org/) and[Kenney.nl](https://kenney.nl/) offer free game assets.
- **Pixel art animation:**[Piskel](https://www.piskelapp.com/) lets you draw animated pixel art for your characters and Objects.
- **Sound effects:**[Freesound.org](https://freesound.org/) has a large library of user-uploaded sounds, and Bfxr makes retro-style game sounds.
- **Music:**[Bensound](https://www.bensound.com/) offers royalty-free tracks.
- **Audio editing:** Audacity is a free, open-source editor for trimming and mixing your own sounds.


## How Long Does It Take?


- **First working prototype:** one to two hours.
- **Something you would show a friend:** a weekend.
- **Something on the App Store:** a few months, most of it spent on art, polish, and testing rather than logic.


## What You Can and Cannot Do for Free


hyperPad Starter is free and lets you build and test one project with the full set of tools. You can learn everything the editor does inside that one project, and you can publish it to the Hub.


Working on more than one project at a time and exporting to the App Store need the paid version, hyperPad, which is a one-time USD $14.99. There is no subscription, and you keep 100% of the revenue from anything you ship.


## Other Free Ways to Make Games


hyperPad is built for iPad. If you're comparing options, here are other free tools people use:


- **Scratch:** great for younger creators and classrooms, though more limited in game complexity.
- **GDevelop:** a free, open-source engine with drag-and-drop logic for Windows, Mac, Linux, web and mobile.
- **Builda:** an iPad and iPhone app for drawing and animating simple games.
- **GameMaker:** a 2D engine for Windows and Mac. Complex behaviors still need code.
- **Defold:** a free engine for desktop, mobile, web and consoles, with a steeper learning curve.
- **Phaser:** a free JavaScript framework for browser games. It requires coding.


## Common Questions


**Can you really make games on an iPad?** Yes. Games built on iPad with hyperPad have shipped to the App Store.


**Do you need to know how to code?** No. You connect Behaviors instead. If you later want to learn to code, the logic you build here maps directly onto the concepts you will meet.


**Do you need a Mac to publish?** No. You Export to the App Store from the iPad.


**What if I cannot draw?** Use the built-in asset library to start. Free game art is easy to find (see the list above), and you can replace placeholder art later.


**Does it work offline?** Yes, building and testing work without a connection.


## Where to Go Next


Once your tapper works, try a second project with one new idea in it: a platformer with a double jump, a rhythm game, or a puzzle with a timer. Each one teaches you a Behavior you did not need before.


A few habits help:


- **Finish small games first.** A polished simple game teaches more than an unfinished big one.
- **Reuse assets and templates.** You don't have to make everything from scratch.
- **Learn from other creators.** Open Source projects in the Hub can be branched, so you can see exactly how someone else built a mechanic.
- **Gameplay before visuals.** Make it fun, then make it pretty.


The hyperPad community on Discord is a good place to get unstuck. For more walkthroughs, see the[hyperPad Blog](https://www.hyperpad.com/blog) and beginner video guides on[YouTube @hyperPad](https://www.youtube.com/@hyperPad) .
